comparisons.peer_summary: The Company has four reportable segments: Data Center (including AI accelerators, CPUs, GPUs, etc.), Client (CPUs, APUs, chipsets for desktops/notebooks), Gaming (discrete GPUs, semi-custom SoCs), and Embedded (embedded CPUs, GPUs, APUs, FPGAs, SOMs).
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and AMD define their core Data Center reporting structures around AI acceleration and server processing hardware, though AMD separates its data center focus into a distinct 'Data Center' segment while NVDA groups it within a broader 'Compute & Networking' segment that also includes automotive and networking-specific products. NVDA explicitly includes 'networking' and 'automotive AI' in its primary compute segment definition, whereas AMD's Data Center segment is strictly defined by server-oriented silicon (CPUs, GPUs, AI accelerators, DPUs, FPGAs) without mentioning automotive or networking hardware as part of that specific segment report line. This highlights a structural difference: NVDA integrates networking and auto-AI into its compute narrative, while AMD isolates compute infrastructure from other verticals.

comparisons.peer_summary: The semiconductor solutions segment provides devices for data center, service provider, and enterprise networking applications, including AI networking, as well as products for mobile, set-top box, broadband access, storage, industrial, and automotive markets. The segment also includes IP licensing.
comparisons.comparison: Both companies highlight 'AI networking' as a key component of their semiconductor strategies in Item 8. However, their segment definitions diverge significantly: NVDA places networking products and AI solutions under the 'Compute & Networking' segment alongside data center compute platforms, whereas AVGO isolates 'AI networking and connectivity' within its 'Semiconductor solutions' segment but distinguishes it by focusing on 'managing the movement of data' (switches, routers, smartNICs) rather than the compute acceleration platforms (GPUs/AI accelerators) that NVDA emphasizes. NVDA's definition includes 'DGX Cloud' and 'automotive' within the same compute bucket, while AVGO's semiconductor solutions cover a wider array of end-markets including mobile, set-top box, and broadband access, showing a broader horizontal product spread compared to NVDA's concentrated compute/AI focus.

comparisons.peer_summary: Business is organized into Intel Products, Intel Foundry, and All other; CCG, DCAI, and Intel Foundry are reportable operating segments, while NEX, Altera, and Mobileye are non-reportable segments with selective disclosure.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and INTC define specific operating segments focused on Data Center and AI workloads. NVDA's 'Compute & Networking' segment directly encompasses 'Data Center accelerated computing platform' and 'NVIDIA AI Enterprise', reflecting a unified compute+software+networking approach. In contrast, INTC separates its Data Center and AI focus into the 'Data Center and AI (DCAI)' segment but also maintains a distinct 'Intel Foundry' reportable segment, reflecting its dual identity as both a designer and a manufacturer. NVDA's definition is product-family centric (Compute & Networking), while INTC's definition is organizational and manufacturing-process centric (DCAI for design revenue, Intel Foundry for manufacturing services), illustrating a fundamental difference in how they report AI-related financial performance.

comparisons.peer_topic: Definition of Compute and Networking Business Unit (CNBU)
comparisons.peer_summary: The Compute and Networking Business Unit includes memory products and solutions sold into the data center, PC, graphics, and networking markets.
comparisons.comparison: While both companies have business units covering 'Compute' and 'Networking' markets, the substance of their definitions differs materially based on their core product offerings. NVDA's 'Compute & Networking' segment focuses on 'accelerated computing platforms,' 'AI Enterprise software,' and 'autonomous driving,' emphasizing active processing and AI infrastructure. MU's 'Compute and Networking Business Unit (CNBU)' is defined by 'memory products and solutions,' highlighting passive or storage-centric components sold into the same data center and networking markets. Thus, while the market labels (Compute/Networking) are similar, the underlying financial drivers (accelerators/AI platforms vs. memory/storage) are distinct, making them related but not directly comparable in terms of the specific business activity defined.
